title: The Neural Crest: Cells That Leave Home

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: The neural crest arises at the border between the neural plate and {{c1::future skin}}.
cards.back: Both arise from ectoderm.
cards.quote: The neural crest forms at the border between the two.
cards.section: A border population that leaves home

cards.front: How does epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition let a neural crest cell leave the neural tube?
cards.back: It loosens adhesion to neighbours, loses epithelial polarity, crosses the basement membrane and becomes a mobile mesenchymal cell.
cards.quote: They loosen their grip on their neighbours, lose the top-to-bottom polarity of an epithelial cell, break through the basement membrane
cards.section: A border population that leaves home

cards.front: In birds and mammals, neural crest normally makes bone and cartilage in the {{c1::head}}.
cards.back: Trunk crest does not normally make skeleton.
cards.quote: In birds and mammals, trunk crest does not normally make skeleton; crest bone and cartilage are a head speciality.
cards.section: A border population that leaves home

cards.front: Which axial neural crest populations give rise to neurons and glia of the gut wall?
cards.back: Vagal and sacral crest; their derivatives form the enteric nervous system.
cards.quote: Where they end up, and what they become, differs along the body:
cards.section: A border population that leaves home

cards.front: What major heart structure does cardiac neural crest help form?
cards.back: The tissue dividing the outflow into the aorta and pulmonary trunk; cardiac crest is part of the vagal level.
cards.quote: Where they end up, and what they become, differs along the body:
cards.section: A border population that leaves home

cards.front: How do a neural crest population’s starting position and later environment jointly influence its fate?
cards.back: Starting position biases its possible fates; signals along its route and at its destination help determine which appear.
cards.quote: Where along the body a crest population starts biases what it can become;
cards.section: A border population that leaves home

cards.front: Why did Platt’s serial sections support an ectodermal contribution to head cartilage without establishing a living cell’s lineage?
cards.back: Low yolk distinguished ectodermal cells in fixed embryos, but successive sections did not follow one labelled living cell or manipulate its fate.
cards.quote: her evidence was indirect, from fixed sections with no living cell labelled or moved.
cards.section: How do you follow a cell that leaves?

cards.front: What intrinsic marker distinguishes quail donor descendants in a chick neural crest graft?
cards.back: A dense chromatin mass associated with the nucleolus, visible with DNA staining and absent in chick nuclei; it persists through cell division.
cards.quote: The mark neither fades nor dilutes as cells divide.
cards.section: Classic experiment: quail-chick chimeras

cards.front: Donor neural crest is grafted at its original axial level and reaches the usual targets. Why can this map destinations without explaining fate choice?
cards.back: Origin and route remain coupled. The experiment shows where cells go but does not separate effects of starting identity from environmental signals.
cards.quote: It cannot show why they become what they do, because origin and route are confounded:
cards.section: Classic experiment: quail-chick chimeras

cards.front: Vagal quail crest transplanted to a chick adrenomedullary site produces sympathetic and adrenal derivatives. What claim about fate does this challenge?
cards.back: That axial origin fixes the population’s fate. The new location changes its output from the usual enteric derivatives.
cards.quote: vagal crest grafted to the adrenomedullary level makes adrenal medulla and sympathetic derivatives.
cards.section: Moving the cells: heterotopic grafts

cards.front: Why does a mixed neural crest graft producing a new cell type not prove that the new environment instructed individual cells to change fate?
cards.back: The environment might instead favour a pre-existing subset already capable of that fate. A population graft cannot distinguish instruction from selection.
cards.quote: The graft cannot say whether it instructed cells that would have become noradrenergic or favoured a subset already able to become cholinergic.
cards.section: Moving the cells: heterotopic grafts

cards.front: A trunk-to-vagal crest graft produces enteric neurons, but most early trunk-to-head grafts produce little or no cartilage. What combined model explains both?
cards.back: Origin biases competence, while the route and destination influence which fates appear. The enteric result shows environmental influence; the cartilage limit shows that environment alone does not determine output.
cards.quote: So the start biases what the cells can make, and the surroundings help choose.
cards.section: Moving the cells: heterotopic grafts

cards.front: A single founder that can produce several cell types is {{c1::multipotent}}.
cards.back: This describes a capacity, not a guarantee that every fate occurs in the embryo.
cards.quote: So some crest cells can make several cell types.
cards.section: One cell, or a mixed population?

cards.front: Why does a single neural crest founder making neurons and melanocytes in culture not establish that it makes both in an embryo?
cards.back: Culture tests capacity under one condition. The embryo’s route and surroundings may allow only one of those fates.
cards.quote: Culture shows what a cell can make under one condition;
cards.section: One cell, or a mixed population?

cards.front: In a hypothetical single-founder crest culture, 190 colonies form; 17 fail crest-marker criteria. Of the remaining colonies, 76 contain both neuronal and non-neuronal cells. What percentage of analysed clones demonstrates multiple cell types?
cards.back: Analysed clones = 190 − 17 = 173. Mixed fraction = 76/173 × 100 = 43.93%, about 44%. This demonstrates capacity in culture, not the frequency of multipotency in embryos.
cards.quote: Others contained several neuron types, non-neuronal cells and melanocytes.
cards.section: One cell, or a mixed population?

cards.front: A single premigratory chick trunk cell is labelled in place, and its descendants later occupy several derivatives. Which conclusion is justified about premigratory crest?
cards.back: Some premigratory cells are multipotent in vivo. One such clone does not establish that the typical cell is broadly multipotent.
cards.quote: Some single clones spread into more than one derivative, and some included cells that stayed in the neural tube.
cards.section: One cell, or a mixed population?

cards.front: How would you test whether the multiple fates seen from isolated crest founders in culture also occur during normal development?
cards.back: Label individual premigratory cells in place with a lasting lineage mark and identify their descendants later. The rules are that culture measures capacity, while in-place tracing measures realised output; the label must persist.
cards.quote: To learn what a cell did make, label it in place and find its descendants later.
cards.section: One cell, or a mixed population?

cards.front: How does the proposed neural crest gene-regulatory network link border signals to migration?
cards.back: BMP, Wnt and FGF activate border genes, then crest genes, then adhesion and movement genes. Untested regulatory arrows remain hypotheses.
cards.quote: The crest genes in turn control the genes that change adhesion and movement and, later, influence fate.
cards.section: Leaving home: an identity first, then a release

cards.front: In premigratory chick neural crest, {{c1::Cadherin-6B}} helps hold cells to their neighbours.
cards.back: Snail2 probably promotes departure at least partly by repressing this adhesion gene.
cards.quote: premigratory chick crest cells are held to their neighbours partly by a cadherin, Cadherin-6B.
cards.section: Leaving home: an identity first, then a release

cards.front: Snail2 is lowered in premigratory chick crest while Cadherin-6B remains intact. What happens to Cadherin-6B RNA and emigration, and why?
cards.back: Cadherin-6B RNA rises and fewer cells leave, because lowering its repressor Snail2 preserves an adhesion brake on departure.
cards.quote: Cadherin-6B RNA should rise, and fewer cells should leave.
cards.section: Leaving home: an identity first, then a release

cards.front: Snail2 knockdown reduces chick crest departure, but that alone does not establish that Cadherin-6B restrains emigration. What independent perturbation tests the proposed brake?
cards.back: Lower Cadherin-6B without lowering Snail2 and measure departure timing. Earlier emigration supports a brake; this was observed in chick.
cards.quote: lowered Cadherin-6B, and crest cells did emigrate early.
cards.section: Leaving home: an identity first, then a release

cards.front: In a hypothetical chick crest experiment, emigration is 40% in controls, 10% after Snail2 knockdown and 25% after combined Snail2/Cadherin-6B knockdown. What fraction of the lost emigration is restored?
cards.back: Loss = 40 − 10 = 30 percentage points. Rescue = 25 − 10 = 15 points. Restored fraction = 15/30 = 0.5, or 50%. This supports partial mediation; other targets or incomplete knockdown could explain the remainder.
cards.quote: other Snail2 targets, or incomplete knockdown, could explain the rest.
cards.section: Leaving home: an identity first, then a release

cards.front: Which major derivatives follow the ventromedial versus later dorsolateral routes of chick trunk neural crest?
cards.back: Ventromedial, through somites: dorsal root ganglia, sympathetic ganglia and adrenal medulla. Later dorsolateral, under skin: mostly melanocytes.
cards.quote: The dorsolateral route, taken later, runs under the skin and gives mostly melanocytes.
cards.section: Steering: a forbidden half and cells that back away

cards.front: How does ephrin-B help confine chick trunk crest migration to the rostral half of each sclerotome?
cards.back: Membrane-bound ephrin-B on caudal-half cells contacts EphB receptors on crest cells. Forward signaling repels the crest cell from the caudal half.
cards.quote: Because both sit in membranes, the signal passes only where a crest cell touches a caudal-half cell.
cards.section: Steering: a forbidden half and cells that back away

cards.front: In a simplified chick trunk model with EphB–ephrin-B as the only caudal repellent, crest cells lose EphB function. What happens to their route, and why?
cards.back: They enter caudal as well as rostral halves because they can no longer detect that repellent. The simplification excludes other guidance cues present in real embryos.
cards.quote: In chick, crest cells carry EphB receptors, and caudal-half sclerotome cells carry ephrin-B, a membrane-bound ligand.
cards.section: Steering: a forbidden half and cells that back away

cards.front: Chick trunk crest avoids ephrin-B stripes. Design a test distinguishing receptor-mediated repulsion from a passive difference in stripe adhesion.
cards.back: Use a blocking, unclustered soluble ephrin-B preparation, with a nonbinding protein control; verify continued motility. Loss of avoidance with the blocker supports receptor signaling because the stripe surface stays unchanged. Specify form and dose: clustered ligand can activate receptors.
cards.quote: A passive adhesion difference would not be relieved by adding ligand, because the stripe surface itself is unchanged.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: What is contact inhibition of locomotion?
cards.back: When two cells touch, they stop moving toward each other and move off in new directions.
cards.quote: two cells that touch stop moving towards each other and head off in new directions.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How do contact inhibition, mutual attraction and a chemoattractant work together in the proposed frog cranial crest migration model?
cards.back: Contact inhibition polarises cells away from contacts; mutual attraction prevents scattering; the Sdf1 gradient gives the group a direction.
cards.quote: Mutual attraction keeps the group from scattering.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the frog cranial crest collective-migration model, mutual attraction is removed but contact inhibition persists. What happens to group cohesion, and why?
cards.back: The group should scatter more readily: contact inhibition still drives cells apart, but attraction no longer counteracts dispersal.
cards.quote: Contact inhibition pushes cells apart and gives each a front.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A hypothetical migrating cell group retains mutual attraction and contact inhibition but loses its only external chemoattractant gradient. What happens to cohesion and directional guidance, and why?
cards.back: Cohesion can persist, but guidance toward the former attractant source is lost. The model assigns attraction to keeping cells together, contact inhibition to polarity and the gradient to direction.
cards.quote: A chemoattractant gives the group a direction.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: What is neural crest coalescence?
cards.back: Migrating crest cells stop and gather into ganglia. How they organise this without a central planner is still poorly understood.
cards.quote: Then the travellers have to stop and gather.
cards.section: Stopping and gathering

cards.front: In a hypothetical ganglion, how could the timing of cluster failure after removing a cell-adhesion protein distinguish roles in cluster initiation and maintenance?
cards.back: Track arrival and initial gathering, then cluster stability. Scattered arrivals support an initiation role; initial clusters that become loose support maintenance. This uses the proposed distinction between starting clusters and holding them together, not an established result for every ganglion.
cards.quote: If it is needed to start clusters, the cells would stay scattered along the route.
cards.section: Stopping and gathering

cards.front: A disorder of neural crest cells is a {{c1::neurocristopathy}}.
cards.back: Different disorders can affect survival, colonisation or differentiation.
cards.quote: A disorder of neural crest cells is a neurocristopathy,
cards.section: Neurocristopathies: tissues that fail together often share a requirement

cards.front: Using rough birth frequencies of 1/5,000 for Hirschsprung disease and 1/42,000 for Waardenburg syndrome, what combined frequency would independence predict?
cards.back: P(both) = (1/5,000) × (1/42,000) = 1/210,000,000: about one in 210 million births. This is an independence benchmark, not the observed frequency.
cards.quote: If the two were independent, both would turn up together in about 1 in 210 million births.
cards.section: Neurocristopathies: tissues that fail together often share a requirement

cards.front: Why can SOX10, EDNRB or EDN3 variants combine distal gut aganglionosis with pigment changes and hearing loss in Waardenburg syndrome type 4?
cards.back: Both enteric precursors and melanocytes require these genes. Inner-ear melanocytes are needed for hearing, so one defective gene can disrupt both lineages.
cards.quote: Each is needed by both enteric precursors and melanocytes, including the melanocytes the inner ear needs for hearing.
cards.section: Neurocristopathies: tissues that fail together often share a requirement

cards.front: Why does slowing a mouth-to-anus colonisation front within a fixed developmental window preferentially leave the distal gut without neurons?
cards.back: The distal gut is reached last. A slower front can run out of time before reaching that end.
cards.quote: The end the front reaches last: a segment at the anal end.
cards.section: Neurocristopathies: tissues that fail together often share a requirement

cards.front: In a fixed-length gut model, a constant-speed crest front normally reaches the anus exactly when its time window closes. What fraction stays empty at 90% or 80% of normal speed?
cards.back: Let normal speed be v and the window T, so L = vT. Empty fraction = 1 − v′T/L = 1 − v′/v. At 0.90v: 0.10 = 10%; at 0.80v: 0.20 = 20%, at the anal end.
cards.why: This is a toy model, not a measured law. Uneven gut growth changes its numbers; real colonisation also depends on division and survival.
cards.quote: a front at 90 percent of normal speed leaves the last 10 percent empty, and one at 80 percent leaves the last 20 percent.
cards.section: Neurocristopathies: tissues that fail together often share a requirement

cards.front: Why can failed distal gut colonisation in Hirschsprung disease occur without a primary defect in cell migration speed?
cards.back: Colonisation also depends on precursor division and survival. A deficit in either can impair front advance without a primary defect in cell movement.
cards.quote: Real front advance also depends on cell division and survival,
cards.section: Neurocristopathies: tissues that fail together often share a requirement

cards.front: Early crest cell death in mouse Treacher Collins models reduces crest numbers, yet the syndrome mainly affects the face. What prediction about developmental timing does this challenge?
cards.back: That an earlier failed step necessarily affects more tissues. Distribution depends on where and when the gene is required, the variant, dose and tissue sensitivity.
cards.quote: it cuts crest numbers early, yet its effects stay mainly in the head and face.
cards.section: Neurocristopathies: tissues that fail together often share a requirement

cards.front: A disorder affects Schwann cells and central oligodendrocytes. Can neural crest ancestry alone explain their joint failure?
cards.back: No. Schwann cells are crest-derived, but central oligodendrocytes are not. Their joint failure points to a gene needed by both cell types; a shared requirement can span distinct lineages.
cards.quote: a shared requirement is not always a shared lineage:
cards.section: Neurocristopathies: tissues that fail together often share a requirement

cards.front: A patient’s pale skin patch contains melanocytes, but they make little or no melanin. Which is the better explanation: failed melanocyte arrival or failed pigment differentiation, and why?
cards.back: Failed pigment differentiation: cells arrived but do not make normal pigment. Loss of melanoblast survival or migration would instead leave patches lacking melanocytes.
cards.quote: Albinism sits at the very end of the chain for crest-derived pigment cells.
cards.section: Neurocristopathies: tissues that fail together often share a requirement

cards.front: Why should the listed neurocristopathies not be assigned to neural crest specification or EMT alone?
cards.back: Animal border-gene roles do not establish specification-only causes for these disorders. Few human disorders trace to EMT alone; the clearest EMT evidence is from chick.
cards.quote: Few human disorders trace to EMT alone either; the clearest evidence on EMT is from chick.
cards.section: Neurocristopathies: tissues that fail together often share a requirement

cards.front: In a mouse Cre lineage-tracing system, Cre permanently switches on a {{c1::reporter gene}} in targeted cells and their descendants.
cards.back: The permanent mark allows descendants to be followed.
cards.quote: Cre switches on a reporter gene permanently in those cells and all their descendants.
cards.section: Genetic lineage tracing

cards.front: A mouse experiment counts only cells reaching the adrenal medulla in the early main crest stream. What later source could make this underestimate crest-derived chromaffin cells, and why?
cards.back: Schwann cell precursors travelling along growing nerves can supply many adrenal chromaffin cells later. Counting only the early stream misses this later crest-derived contribution.
cards.quote: They reach their targets along nerves, a later route than the two main streams.
cards.section: A second, later source of trunk derivatives

cards.front: Mouse crest enters both sclerotome halves after loss of one caudal repellent, yet ganglia remain segmented; ganglion segmentation fails only after two pathways are lost. What causal claim is too strong?
cards.back: That segmented migration is required for segmented ganglia. The rule is that migration and ganglion segmentation can be separated; combining this with multiple guidance cues supports redundant contributions rather than a single sufficient explanation.
cards.quote: Segmented migration is thought to help segment the dorsal root ganglia, but the two can be separated.
cards.section: Segmented migration and segmented ganglia
